clinicalPearls: A rare aggressive malignancy of cells showing morphological and immunophenotypic features of mature tissue macrophages (histiocytes)
May present at nodal, extranodal or disseminated sites, with common involvement of the gastrointestinal tract, skin, soft tissue and lymph nodes
Systemic symptoms such as fever, weight loss and cytopenias are frequent, and disseminated disease carries a poor outlook
The tumour cells are large and pleomorphic and express histiocytic markers such as CD163, CD68 and lysozyme while lacking B-cell, T-cell, dendritic-cell, melanocytic and epithelial markers
It can arise in association with, or transform from, other haematological neoplasms such as follicular lymphoma or chronic lymphocytic leukaemia, sometimes sharing clonal genetic features
Recurrent activating mutations in the MAPK pathway, including BRAF and other kinase genes, occur in a proportion of cases and may offer targeted-therapy opportunities
Localised disease may be treated with surgery and radiotherapy, while disseminated disease requires systemic chemotherapy, generally with limited durable success
reference.pathophysiology: Histiocytic sarcoma is a clonal proliferation of cells committed to the macrophage/histiocyte lineage, retaining the antigen-expression profile of mature tissue macrophages such as CD163 and CD68. In a subset of cases the tumour is clonally related to a preceding or concurrent lymphoid neoplasm, reflecting a phenomenon of lineage plasticity or transdifferentiation in which a committed lymphoid clone acquires a histiocytic phenotype while sharing molecular hallmarks such as immunoglobulin gene rearrangements. Recurrent activating alterations of the RAS-RAF-MEK-ERK (MAPK) signalling pathway drive proliferation in many cases. The malignant histiocytes infiltrate tissues destructively and disseminate widely, producing the aggressive, often treatment-resistant clinical behaviour.
additionalDifferentials: Diffuse large B-cell lymphoma or anaplastic large cell lymphoma
Follicular and interdigitating dendritic cell sarcoma
Langerhans cell histiocytosis and Langerhans cell sarcoma
Reactive histiocytic proliferations and haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
additionalInvestigations: Biopsy with immunohistochemistry showing CD163, CD68 and lysozyme positivity and absence of lymphoid, dendritic and epithelial markers
Clonality and molecular studies, including assessment of relationship to any associated lymphoid neoplasm
Molecular testing for BRAF and other MAPK-pathway mutations to guide targeted therapy
PET-CT and cross-sectional imaging for staging
Bone marrow examination and full blood count
Exclusion of reactive histiocytic and haemophagocytic conditions
redFlags: Rapidly progressive disseminated disease with systemic symptoms
Bone marrow failure with severe cytopenias
Bulky or destructive extranodal masses causing organ compromise
Features of haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis complicating the disease
reference.prognosis: Localised histiocytic sarcoma may be controlled with surgery and radiotherapy, but disseminated or high-stage disease is aggressive with poor survival despite chemotherapy; identification of targetable MAPK-pathway mutations offers a potential avenue for improved outcomes in selected patients.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing the tumour as anaplastic lymphoma, carcinoma or dendritic-cell sarcoma without a full histiocytic marker panel
Failing to recognise clonal relationship to an associated lymphoid neoplasm
Overlooking targetable BRAF or other MAPK-pathway mutations
Confusing malignant disease with reactive histiocytosis or haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis
Underestimating the aggressive behaviour of disseminated disease
references: British and international guidance on histiocytic and dendritic neoplasms
management: Localised, resectable disease is treated with curative intent using complete surgical resection as primary treatment
Adjuvant radiotherapy is considered after surgery for close or positive margins, bulky lesions, or sites where wide resection is not feasible
Locally advanced or marginally resectable disease can be managed with radiotherapy alone or combined with systemic therapy for local control when surgery would be disfiguring or incomplete
Disseminated, multifocal, or high-stage disease shifts intent to disease control, with systemic therapy as the mainstay
First-line systemic therapy for disseminated disease is typically anthracycline-based combination chemotherapy, similar to regimens used in aggressive lymphoma or soft tissue sarcoma
On progression, alternative cytotoxic combinations used in aggressive lymphoma or sarcoma can be considered
Tumours with activating MAPK-pathway mutations (such as BRAF) may be treated with BRAF-directed or combined BRAF/MEK-directed targeted therapy
Any coexisting lymphoid clone in tumours arising from or associated with another haematological neoplasm should be assessed and treated, since it may drive relapse independently
Clinical trial enrolment should be considered at any line given the absence of a standard-of-care regimen established by controlled trials
Monitoring includes baseline and interval cross-sectional and or PET imaging, with frequency guided by initial stage and risk
Regular full blood count is used to monitor for disease- and treatment-related cytopenias and marrow involvement
Clinical monitoring for systemic B symptoms and for features of secondary haemophagocytic lymphohistiocytosis is recommended, as this can complicate the disease course
Referral to a haemato-oncology or sarcoma multidisciplinary team with expert haematopathology review is warranted for any suspected or confirmed case

Refer for molecular testing of BRAF and other MAPK-pathway alterations at diagnosis or relapse, and refer early to a centre with clinical trial access given generally poor outcomes in disseminated disease
